paragraphs.text: A discourse by the blessed apostle Peter on admonition.

When a large crowd was gathered around the apostle Peter, wanting to hear a word of instruction from him, he spoke and said to them, “My brothers, do not become attached to anything in this world. Instead, take care for your lives, so that when you are summoned to depart from here, you will be found ready. And see that nothing is better than a good name, and no yoke is heavier or harder than worldly anxiety. I will show you what these things are like.

“In a certain city there was an important man who was very rich. He had many good servants. But two members of his household did wrong and despised his command. Their master became angry with them and banished them from his presence to a distant land. One of the servants whom he had banished went and had children in the country to which he had gone. He planted vineyards and a garden and set up a bakery for himself. He also built many buildings. But the other servant gathered all his trading profits and converted them into gold. He gave it to a craftsman who worked in gold. He decorated it and made that gold into a crown. The servant said to that craftsman, ‘I am a servant, and I have a master and his son. Engrave these masters of mine on the crown.’ He did so and said to that servant, ‘Here is the crown. Remember to put it on your head.’ The servant answered him, ‘Take your payment for the crown, for I have a time when I will put it on.’

“After a long time, the day came for these servants to be called to account. Their master sent a harsh and merciless servant after them. His master said to him, ‘If you do not [?] bring them within seven days, you will face great danger.’ Then the servant who had been sent set out with great haste. He went to that country, reached those servants, and seized them. He said to them, ‘Your master has sent me after you.’ First he seized the one who had built buildings, planted vineyards, and acquired possessions. He said to him, ‘Get up; let us go, because he has sent me after you.’ The man answered him sorrowfully, ‘Yes, I am coming.’ But afterward he said to him, ‘Be patient with me a little, until I sell everything I have acquired and built here, so that whatever I receive may go with me to my master.’ The servant who had been sent after him said to him, ‘I cannot be patient with you even a little, because I have been given a deadline of only seven days to bring you back. If I delay for you, I will face great danger. Because I fear my master’s threat, I cannot wait for you.’

Then that servant answered, ‘Woe to me, for I was not found ready for this journey!’ The one who had been sent after him answered, ‘I cannot be patient with you even a little, because there are only seven days.’ And he said to him, ‘You wicked servant! Did you not know that you have a master, that you had been banished by him, and that whenever he remembers you, he sends for you? Why did you plant vineyards for yourself, build buildings, and acquire possessions in this country to which you came? Now you have been found unprepared, and you have gone out empty-handed, leaving behind everything for which you labored and toiled.’ Then that servant wept and said, ‘Woe to me! Woe to me! What has happened to me!’ I was acting as though I would spend all my days in this place to which I had been banished. I did not know that my master was going to send for me. That is why I acquired all these possessions, yet none of them has benefited me. And my master is demanding an account of my work.” Then the one who had been sent for him hurriedly brought him out, without his taking anything with him to his master.

But when the other servant heard that someone had been sent for him, he immediately got up, ready and prepared, and took the gold crown he had made. He went ahead to the road along which the one sent for them would travel. He sat there waiting for him until he came to fetch him. When he came to him, he said to him, “Your master has sent me for you.” The servant said to him, “I am ready to go joyfully. For I have nothing here to hold me back. What I do have is light and small, for I have nothing except this gold crown. I prepared it for myself while I was always waiting and praying that I might receive forgiveness, and that my master might have mercy on me and send someone to take me away from this foreign place, lest some of the people of this country envy me and take this crown away from me. Now my prayer and petition have been delivered. Get up, then, and let us go without delay.”

Then both those servants came with the one who had been sent for them. When their master saw them, he said to the one who had brought nothing with him, “Where is all the fruit of your work during this whole time you have been away from me?” That servant answered his master, “My master, you sent a harsh servant for me. I asked him to give me time to sell what I owned and bring the proceeds in my hands to you, but he would not let me.” Then his master answered, “You wicked servant! Only now, after I sent for you, did you remember to sell your possessions? Why did you not consider that you had been banished by me to that place, and reflect and see that everything you acquired there would be of no benefit to you?” Then his master became angry with him and ordered him to be bound hand and foot and sent to the regions of darkness.

His master called the other servant, who had made the gold crown, and said to him, “Where is the fruit of your work during all this time?” He answered his master, “My master, I was always watching and waiting for the time when you would remember me and send for me. For this reason I gathered together all the proceeds of my work and made myself this crown to present to you as an offering.” His master answered him, “Good and faithful servant! From the crown you made for yourself, it is clear that you loved freedom. For a crown belongs to free people, and you did not dare to put it on your head without your master’s command. Since you desired freedom, you shall have what you desired.” Then his master placed him over many servants.

So it is also with those who are called servants of the heavenly bridegroom. The master of the house is our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of all creation, who banished us to this place because of our sins. We live here as though in exile, for we are not left here forever. For the end comes for each one of us, and we are led away from here. A harsh and merciless messenger is sent, namely death. And when he comes to take away the soul of the sinner who has amassed for himself a wealth of many sins, He presses her hard, and terror falls upon him. She begins to plead and say, “Be patient with me, my lord, for a little while. I will repent and atone for the sins I committed in my body.” But Death will not be persuaded, because his appointed time has come, and Death cannot leave him. So if he departs in his sins, with no righteous deeds accompanying him, he is sent by God to the place of torment. But the soul that has good deeds does not fear Death. Instead, she goes with him joyfully, seeing and saying, “There is nothing holding me back in this world, because all my possessions are with me: the good and great name I have acquired, which is virginity, and the righteous deeds in which I am clothed. And I ask the one who was sent after her not to leave her in this place, lest the inhabitants of the place, who are demons, rise up and capture her, and take from her the glorious crown of her virginity, which she acquired through toil and suffering.” And when that soul leaves her body, she is led away and goes to the bridegroom amid songs of praise, until she reaches the regions of the Father’s house. He sees her and rejoices in her, and establishes her in life, together with the body in which she labored, over many regions.

There was also a certain hermit in the outer wilderness who lived in a cave. He devoted himself diligently to every aspect of the solitary life. He earned his bread through the labor of his hands. He was very rich in [?] and had grown rich in spiritual victories. He looked at his good deeds and became very confident in himself. But he had been requested from God for testing, as Job had been.

And he began to tempt him, appearing to him in the evening in the likeness of a beautiful woman who had lost her way in the wilderness. She found the door open, rushed into the cave, and fell at the hermit’s feet. She begged him for mercy and [?], claiming that evening had overtaken her and she did not know where to go. He felt pity and compassion for her—something he ought not to have done—and received her into his cave. He began asking her how she had lost her way. But as she told him about her wandering, she cast words of seduction into him, corrupting his mind. She prolonged her conversation with him very sweetly, and shamelessly stirred up evil desire in him. They talked a great deal to one another, and shameful laughter passed between them. She led him astray with her many words. Then she gently stretched out her hand to touch his hand, his beard, and his neck. At last she captured the hermit completely.

For inwardly he was turning over many thoughts, imagining that the matter was already in his hands. Thinking that it was a quiet time and that he could satisfy his desire without fear, he now surrendered to his inclination and became a servant of the evil whisperer. Having utterly despised his own life, he now dared to have intercourse with her. But suddenly she cried out loudly and slipped out of his hands, vanishing like smoke. Loud laughter from many demons could be heard in the air. They mocked, rebuked, and taunted him because he had gone astray. They jeered at him loudly, saying, “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled!” And you who have been raised up to the abyss, remain until morning in deep groaning and bitter mourning. And after you have lamented, rise, bearing the burden of the night in inconsolable mourning, and wait all day in choking tears and incessant lamentation.

While pangs gripped him, he was giving up hope—something he should not have done—and turning back to the world. For this is the crafty one's tactic: when he fights and defeats his adversary, he then draws him into madness and cuts off the strength of his soul, so that he can no longer regain his strength and rise. And for this reason, my children, it is not good for you to live near a settlement, nor to look at women or converse with them. For the memory of them is not forgotten, the memory that we seek in our minds through sight and conversation. Nor is it right for us to give up hope and let our soul sink through unbelief. Look, many who neglected their salvation and sank into the mire of sin were, through their repentance, found worthy of God's mercy.
